name: Underdark Deep
lines: Ask for work at the 📋 Hiring here board, and your badge will open it.
Main Drift · 108 m
Shot-firer only past this line when the horn blows
Signals to the winding engine
4: men riding · 9: danger
the cage, the signals, who is down
Take a lamp, leave your tally
Count them out, count them back
⚠ The Old Workings are closed
Boarded off off the West Drift
Nobody goes past the boards
Snap time: one bell
Ore pass to the level below
Mind the cribs: never pull a crib timber
Keep the sump down or the level drowns
Engine oiled every shift
Unsafe roof · Bad air · KEEP OUT
Hesketh Marrow, the mine foreman
Mind your head and keep to the drift. Who sent you down? Never mind: you're here now. Lamp from the lamp room, tally on the board, and you'll be fine.
Ada Pennock, the onsetter

the onsetter at the pit bottom: she signals the winding engine with the bell, loads the cage and keeps the book of who is underground. Brisk, funny, never misses a count; she explains real mine signals and how a cage and winding engine work.
Name for the book? Everyone down gets written in and written out. That's how we know nobody's left behind.
Old Joss Tallow, the lamp keeper

the lamp keeper: very old, gentle, a little deaf; he trims and fills every lamp and knows every story about the mine. He explains how real miners' safety lamps work (the gauze that stops a flame lighting firedamp gas, invented in 1815). He remembers Tamsin Rook, who 'went where the cold air came from' and came back smiling.
Here's your lamp. Wick's trimmed, oil's full. Bring it back lit, mind. If it ever burns blue and tall, you get out.
Rafe Kettering, the shot-firer
the shot-firer at No. 1 Face, who drills the holes and fires the charges; calm, exact and very serious about the warning horn. He explains how rock is drilled and blasted in a real mine, safely.
Stand back of the line when the horn goes. Three blasts before, one after. Otherwise: welcome to the face.
Ned Slack, the pump man
the pump man who keeps the West Drift's sump pumped out; cheerful, oily, and in love with his engine. He explains how real mine pumps keep water out of deep mines.
Hear her? Thump, hiss, thump. Every minute she lifts a bathtub of water out of this level. Lovely engine.
The boarded-up Old Workings
An old daybook on a crate
The boards are nailed fast. One of them, near the left, looks loose. (Look closer: press E.)
A rockfall. Loose stones, piled to the roof. A cold breath of air comes through the cracks between them.
Five planks nailed across an old adit, and a sign: DANGER, OLD WORKINGS, KEEP OUT. Beyond them, in the dark, the rusted rails of a narrower, older track go off into the rock.
The air coming between the planks is cold. Down here, everywhere else, the rock is warm.
The loose plank is swung aside; there is room to squeeze past.
Squeeze past the loose plank
It swings aside on one nail
The plank swings aside on its one nail. You squeeze through into the Old Workings. Watch your head.
Tamsin Rook's daybook
Damp at the edges, the ink gone brown. A miner's notes, long ago.

Third week. Followed the cold air south past the old rails. It comes from the fall at the end of the squeeze. Shifted a few stones: there is a room behind, and the walls are not ours. They are cut smooth, older than any mine.

Fourth week. The far wall is carved: a ring of sixteen marks, a tall spire in the middle, a spider with its legs spread. Every mark is cold but one. The one that is warm is shaped like the spider's eye.
I pressed it. I will not write here what is on the other side. I will only say: be courteous, and come back.
The fallen stones are pushed aside. The squeeze goes on east.

Loose stones fill the squeeze to the roof. They are not heavy, and they are not wedged: somebody has moved them before. Cold air breathes through the gaps, and very faintly, beyond them, something glints violet.
Clear the loose stones
A little at a time
You lift the stones away , one by one…
The way is clear. The squeeze goes on east, and the cold air with it.
a ring of three dots
the marks round the spire's top
a small round mark, the spider's own eye
a crescent, horns down
the mark under the spire
beside the spider's leg
in the ring, the topmost mark
the lowest in the ring

The chamber's far wall is smooth rock, carved: a ring of sixteen marks, a tall spire, a spider with its legs spread. Older than the mine; older, maybe, than the city above. You lay your hand on the marks, one after another.
Cold stone. Nothing happens.
Warm under your hand. A grinding, deep in the rock. The whole wall is sinking into the floor…
First among the Houses
judges and keepers of the law
The Court of Judgement
House Vaelith has given Zhaelvorn its eldest Matron for nine hundred years. In Old Ylmarr they kept the Stone of Law; when the old city fell into the Riven Deep they carried it out on their backs.
We hold the city together
weavers of the web bridges and the silk
Every web bridge in Zhaelvorn was spun by House Ostrael. Their founder wove the first rope across the Riven Deep the night Old Ylmarr fell, and everyone crossed on it.
mages of the deep arts
The Faerglow Laboratory
House Myrrhen founded the Duskwell Academy. They study the faerglow, the faint light in the rock, and the old songs that make stone remember.
The blade keeps the peace
blademasters of the Spire Guard
House Zelvane trains the Spire Guard in the Thornyard. They say a Zelvane blade has not been drawn in anger in three hundred years, which is exactly how they like it.
Every tunnel, known
mapmakers and scholars
House Ithrael keeps the Great Chart, a map of every tunnel within a month's walk, cut into silver plates. Ysra of the Halfway Market learned her craft here.
Fair weight, long friendship
The Counting House
House Korvaen trades with Glimmerdeep, the Sunless Sea and the dwarves of Stonehallow. Their scales are the only ones every race of the deep trusts.
First into the dark
lizard riders and scouts
The Lizard Stables
House Sablethorn rides the great cave lizards that walk up walls. Their scouts found the Thanes' Road to the dwarves, and keep it safe.
Seat of the Council of Matrons
Enter in peace, and keep it
The Nightbloom perfumer
Silver of Zhaelvorn
Fair weight, by order of House Korvaen
The Duskwell Academy
The circle of calm
The circle of light
The circle of the stone-songs
The Practice Court
Duskwell Academy: shadow, light and stone
Training grounds of the Spire Guard
shoot at the butts
The Thornyard Barracks
The barracks doors
The Thornyard Barracks.
Matron Ilvaryn of House Vaelith

the eldest of the Matrons and head of the Council of Matrons, who rule Zhaelvorn from the Matron Spire; stately, sharp, patient, quietly amused by surface folk. You speak with formal courtesy and expect it back. You are proud of the seven Great Houses, each living in its own great stalactite, and of the city's history back to Old Ylmarr across the Riven Deep.
A surface-walker, in Zhaelvorn. You came through the old door, then. Few find it; fewer are let through it. Speak, and speak well.
Zarith, a blademaster of the Spire Guard

a disciplined, dry-humoured captain of House Zelvane who trains recruits in the Thornyard and keeps the city gate. You respect skill and honesty and have no patience for boasting. You will happily explain the rules of the city, and tell visitors about the Thornyard's archery butts.
Halt, and be welcome, in that order. Weapons stay sheathed in Zhaelvorn. Now: what brings a surface-walker down the long stair?
Velra, a web-weaver

a merchant of House Ostrael who weaves cloth from the silk of the giant spiders the city keeps; warm, talkative, a shrewd trader, proud of her craft, with a stall in the Silk Bazaar. You love explaining how spider silk is gathered and woven.
Silk, friend! Spider silk, finer than anything the surface spins and stronger than steel wire, thread for thread. Come and feel it.
Nym, a young scout

a curious young scout of House Sablethorn who has always wanted to see the surface: the sun, the sky, rain. You ask the visitor lots of questions about the world above and tell them about the tunnels, the lizards of House Sablethorn, the fungus forest and the Thanes' Road to the dwarves of Stonehallow.
Wait, you're from up there? Is it true the roof is blue? And there's a lamp in it so bright you can't look at it? Tell me everything.
Sorrith, keeper of the Spire library

a scholarly mage of House Myrrhen who keeps the city's records cut into stone tablets in the Matron Spire, and studies the faerglow, the faint violet light in the rock. Gentle, absent-minded, delighted by questions. You teach the Lore of the Dead at the Duskwell Academy two days a week (the Summon Wraith spell).
Ah, a visitor. Have you noticed the rock here glows, very faintly? We call it the faerglow. Nobody knows quite what it is. I have theories.
a guard at the doors of
Welcome to the doors of
of the Silk Bazaar

in the Silk Bazaar of Zhaelvorn, a market along the avenue from the city gate to the Court of the Matron Spire. You are friendly to buyers, proud of your wares, and happy to explain how you make them.
Mistress Iriel of the Duskwell Academy

a teacher of the deep arts at the Duskwell Academy (House Myrrhen founded it). You teach Fear and the Dark (the Dread spell) and Soul Drain in the Practice Hall: dark and dangerous fighting magic that works on any foe, beast or dreamer. Each lesson also teaches the real science underneath. Stern, calm, a little unsettling, and welcoming to surface students brave enough to learn.
The circles are open. Step into one and I will teach you something the stone already knows.
Captain Vessa Zelvane

the captain who runs the Thornyard, training grounds of the Spire Guard; brisk, fair and encouraging, with a laugh like a dropped shield. You invite visitors to try the archery butts, watch the sparring, or see the lizard riders of House Sablethorn on their track. You care most about discipline and looking after each other.
Visitor! You're standing on my yard, so you may as well train. The butts are by the far wall: shoot from the white line.
Shadow and Illusion
Light travels in straight lines, so anything solid in its way throws a shadow. The nearer the thing is to the lamp, the bigger its shadow.
An 'illusion' is the eye being honest about light that is being clever: a mirror, a lens, a bent ray in water. The deep arts call it shadow-weaving; the surface calls it optics.
Try it: hold a hand between a lamp and a wall, and move it towards the lamp. Watch the shadow grow.
A hex is the oldest weapon of the deep: a mark cut into the dark that makes a foe weaker every moment it clings. Duskwell teaches it as a fighting art, not a game.
The real thing behind it is slow harm: a bite, a burn or a sickness hurts more over time than in one blow. That is why the Hex of Withering keeps working long after it lands.

Every House of Zhaelvorn guards its door with its sigil: Vaelith's crown, Ostrael's web, Myrrhen's star, Zelvane's blades, Ithrael's compass, Korvaen's scales, Sablethorn's thorn. Cross one uninvited and you will learn why.
Fear is a body's alarm: the heart races, the breath goes short, and the legs want to run before the mind has decided anything. The Dread spell rings that alarm in a foe.
Most hunting beasts are cautious by nature: something that seems bigger and stranger than itself makes it back away. That is why Dread drives beasts off, and why dreamers feel it as a blow.
In the deep dark, the eyes see almost nothing and the ears make up the rest. Mages of Duskwell learn to be the thing in the dark that others are afraid of.
Sorrith of the Spire library
The deep has buried many: miners, soldiers of the old wars, travellers lost in the Riven Deep. Zhaelvorn remembers them, and Duskwell teaches how to call one back to fight for you.
A wraith is a shade of someone long gone, held together by the caller's will. It obeys for as long as the caller can hold it, and no longer: twenty breaths at most.
The real lesson under it: caves keep things. Bones and footprints in cave mud have lasted tens of thousands of years, because no rain or sun reaches them.
Sound travels through rock about fifteen times faster than through air. Put your ear to a long stone wall and you hear footsteps before you hear them through the air.
Miners once listened to the rock to know if a roof was about to fall: it creaks and 'talks' first.
The Echoing Hollow in the west of the cavern is a ring of stones that answer when you call out: an echo is your own voice coming back off the rock.
Mistress Vhessa of House Ostrael
Spider silk is a protein, spun as a liquid and pulled into a thread as it leaves the spider. For its weight it is stronger than steel and it can stretch a third longer before it snaps.
A spider spins different silks for different jobs: a dry, strong one for the spokes of a web, a sticky, stretchy one for the spiral that catches prey.
Venom is not poison you eat: it is made to be delivered by a bite or a sting. Some spider venoms are now studied to make medicines for pain and for the heart.
The Hall of Mirrors
A flat mirror makes an image that seems to stand as far behind the glass as you stand in front of it. Left and right look swapped; up and down do not.
Two mirrors facing each other make images of images, each a little dimmer: a hall that seems to go on forever.
A curved mirror can make a thing look bigger, smaller or upside down. That is why a spoon shows your face both ways.
The Practice Circles
Stand still and breathe slowly: four counts in, four counts out. The first thing any mage of the deep learns is to be calm in the dark.
Your eyes take about twenty minutes to get used to darkness fully; the cells that see in dim light (rods) need time to recharge.
That is why the circles glow so softly: bright light would undo twenty minutes of patience in a moment.
